title: Directing
summary: Directing is the process of instructing, guiding, communicating, motivating and leading people to achieve organisational goals. This chapter covers the features, importance and elements of directing: supervision, motivation (Maslow's need hierarchy and financial and non-financial incentives), leadership styles, and communication with its types, barriers and ways to improve it.

notes.heading: Meaning and Features of Directing
notes.html:
Directing means instructing, guiding, communicating and inspiring people in the organisation so that they work towards its objectives. It is the heart of the management process because it initiates action.

  1. Initiates action – plans are put into action through directing.
  2. Takes place at every level – every manager, from the CEO to the supervisor, directs subordinates.
  3. Continuous process – it goes on throughout the life of the organisation.
  4. Flows from top to bottom – it starts at the top level and flows downward through the hierarchy.

notes.heading: Importance of Directing
notes.html:
1. Initiates action – helps employees start work towards goals.
  2. Integrates employees' efforts – links individual efforts to organisational goals.
  3. Means of motivation – inspires employees to realise their full potential.
  4. Facilitates implementation of changes – effective communication and leadership reduce resistance to change.
  5. Brings stability and balance – through leadership, motivation and communication, it balances different interests in the organisation.

Memory aid: I-I-M-C-S – Initiate, Integrate, Motivate, Change, Stability.

notes.heading: Elements of Directing: Supervision
notes.html:
The four elements are supervision, motivation, leadership and communication (memory aid: SMLC).

Supervision means overseeing the subordinates at work; the supervisor is the link between workers and management.

Importance of supervision:

  • Maintains day-to-day contact and friendly relations with workers.
  • Acts as a link between workers and management.
  • Plays a key role in maintaining group unity and resolving disputes.
  • Ensures performance of work as per targets.
  • Provides on-the-job training to workers.
  • Builds high morale through good leadership.
  • Analyses work and gives feedback to management.

notes.heading: Motivation and Maslow's Need Hierarchy
notes.html:
Motivation is the process of stimulating people to act to accomplish desired goals. Key terms: motive (inner state that energises behaviour), motivation (process of stimulating), motivators (techniques such as pay, promotion, recognition).

Features: internal feeling; produces goal-directed behaviour; can be positive (rewards) or negative (punishment); complex process (individuals differ).

Maslow's Need Hierarchy (from lowest to highest):

  1. Physiological needs – food, shelter, clothing; basic salary.
  2. Safety/security needs – job security, stable income, pension.
  3. Affiliation/belonging (social) needs – affection, acceptance, friendship.
  4. Esteem needs – self-respect, status, recognition, attention.
  5. Self-actualisation needs – becoming what one is capable of; growth, achievement.

Assumptions: behaviour depends on needs; needs are in hierarchical order; a satisfied need no longer motivates; a person moves to the next higher level only when the lower need is satisfied.

Memory aid: Please Send All Executives Somewhere – Physiological, Safety, Affiliation, Esteem, Self-actualisation.

notes.heading: Financial and Non-financial Incentives
notes.html:
Financial incentives (directly or indirectly measurable in money):

  • Pay and allowances – basic pay, dearness allowance, regular increments.
  • Productivity-linked wage incentives – piece rate, bonus linked to output.
  • Bonus – incentive over and above salary.
  • Profit sharing – a share in profits of the firm.
  • Co-partnership / stock option – shares offered to employees at a price lower than market price (ESOP).
  • Retirement benefits – provident fund, pension, gratuity.
  • Perquisites – car, medical aid, company accommodation, children's education.

Non-financial incentives (satisfy psychological, social and emotional needs):

  • Status – rank or position in the organisation.
  • Organisational climate – individual autonomy, reward orientation, consideration to employees.
  • Career advancement opportunity – promotion and growth paths.
  • Job enrichment – designing jobs with greater variety, autonomy and challenge.
  • Employee recognition programmes – e.g. 'employee of the month', certificates.
  • Job security – stability of employment.
  • Employee participation – involving employees in decisions (joint committees, quality circles).
  • Employee empowerment – giving more autonomy and powers to subordinates.

notes.heading: Leadership and Leadership Styles
notes.html:
Leadership is the process of influencing the behaviour of people to make them strive voluntarily towards group objectives.

Features: ability to influence others; aims to bring change in behaviour; shows interpersonal relations between leader and followers; exercised to achieve common goals; continuous process.

BasisAutocraticDemocratic (Participative)Laissez-faire (Free-rein)
Decision-makingLeader aloneLeader with group consultationGroup itself
CommunicationOne-way, top-downTwo-wayFree flow
Role of leaderCommands and expects complianceDevelops action plans with the groupSupports, provides information
Suitable whenSubordinates are untrained or quick decisions neededSubordinates are competent and cooperativeSubordinates are highly skilled and self-motivated

notes.heading: Communication: Formal and Informal
notes.html:
Communication is the process of exchange of ideas, views, facts and feelings between two or more persons to create common understanding. Elements: sender, message, encoding, media, decoding, receiver, feedback, noise.

Formal communication follows the official chain of command; may be vertical (upward/downward) or horizontal (lateral). Networks: single chain, wheel (all subordinates communicate through one superior), circle, free flow, inverted V.

Informal communication (grapevine) arises out of social interaction and spreads fast. Networks: single strand, gossip (one person tells all), probability (random), cluster (to trusted persons, most popular).

BasisFormal CommunicationInformal Communication
MeaningThrough official channelsThrough unofficial channels
SpeedSlowFast
ReliabilityReliable and authenticLess reliable; may spread rumours
RecordsUsually written recordsUsually oral, no record
FlexibilityRigidFlexible

notes.heading: Barriers to Communication and Improving Communication
notes.html:
1. Semantic barriers (problems in encoding and decoding): badly expressed message; symbols with different meanings; faulty translations; unclarified assumptions; technical jargon; body language and gesture decoding.

2. Psychological barriers: premature evaluation; lack of attention; loss by transmission and poor retention; distrust.

3. Organisational barriers: organisational policy; rules and regulations; status; complexity in organisation structure; organisational facilities.

4. Personal barriers: fear of challenge to authority; lack of confidence of superior in subordinates; unwillingness to communicate; lack of proper incentives.

Memory aid: SPOP – Semantic, Psychological, Organisational, Personal.

Improving communication: clarify ideas before communicating; communicate according to the needs of the receiver; consult others before communicating; be aware of language, tone and content; convey things of help and value to listeners; ensure proper feedback; communicate for the present as well as the future; follow up communications; be a good listener.

mcqs.q: Rohit, a sales manager, wants a stable job with a pension plan after his retirement. Which need of Maslow's hierarchy is he trying to satisfy?
mcqs.explanation: Job security and pension relate to safety/security needs.

mcqs.q: A company offers its employees shares at ₹200 when the market price is ₹350. This incentive is:
mcqs.explanation: Offering shares below market price is co-partnership / stock option, a financial incentive.

mcqs.q: The manager of a design studio lets highly skilled designers take their own decisions and only provides resources. Which leadership style is this?
mcqs.explanation: When the group makes its own decisions and the leader only supports, it is laissez-faire (free-rein) leadership.

mcqs.q: An engineer explained a new process to workers using technical terms they did not understand. Which barrier to communication is this?
mcqs.explanation: Technical jargon is a semantic barrier, arising in encoding and decoding.

mcqs.q: 'Employee of the month' awards given to the best performers are an example of:
mcqs.explanation: Publicly appreciating good work is an employee recognition programme, a non-financial incentive.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT an element of directing?
mcqs.explanation: The elements of directing are supervision, motivation, leadership and communication; staffing is a separate function.

mcqs.q: In which communication network do all subordinates communicate only through one central superior?
mcqs.explanation: In the wheel network, the superior acts as the hub through whom all communication passes.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Directing flows from top to bottom.
Reason (R): Every manager directs his immediate subordinates and receives directions from his superior.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Since directions are given by superiors to subordinates down the hierarchy, directing flows downward.

mcqs.q: A manager stopped listening when an employee started describing a problem, because he thought he already knew the issue. Which barrier is this?
mcqs.explanation: Forming a judgement before hearing the full message is premature evaluation, a psychological barrier.

mcqs.q: Which need in Maslow's hierarchy is satisfied by a job that gives a person the chance to achieve his full potential?
mcqs.explanation: Becoming what one is capable of becoming is self-actualisation.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Informal communication is always unreliable and should be stopped by managers.
Reason (R): Informal communication spreads very fast.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
mcqs.explanation: A is false: the grapevine cannot be stopped and can be used by managers to spread useful information quickly. R is true.

mcqs.q: A production head consults his team before finalising the shift schedule and takes their suggestions seriously. Identify the leadership style.
mcqs.explanation: Consulting the group and taking decisions jointly is democratic (participative) leadership.

questions.q: Name the highest-level need in Maslow's need hierarchy.

questions.answerHtml: Grapevine is the informal communication network that arises out of social interaction among employees and spreads information rapidly in any direction.

questions.q: Explain any three features of directing.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Initiates action – directing is the function that sets plans into action.
  2. Takes place at every level – every manager, from top to supervisor, directs his subordinates.
  3. Continuous process – it continues throughout the life of the organisation, irrespective of the people occupying managerial positions.

1. Status – a higher rank or position satisfies esteem needs of employees.
  2. Job enrichment – jobs with greater variety, autonomy and challenge provide opportunity for growth.
  3. Employee participation – involving employees in decision-making gives them a sense of belonging and importance.

questions.q: Explain Maslow's need hierarchy theory of motivation.
questions.answerHtml:
Abraham Maslow arranged human needs in a hierarchy of five levels:

  1. Physiological needs – basic needs for survival such as food, shelter and clothing; satisfied through basic salary.
  2. Safety/security needs – protection from physical and emotional harm; satisfied through job security, stable income and pension.
  3. Affiliation/belonging needs – need for affection, acceptance and friendship; satisfied through good relations with colleagues.
  4. Esteem needs – self-respect, autonomy, status, recognition and attention.
  5. Self-actualisation needs – the drive to become what one is capable of becoming; includes growth and self-fulfilment.

Assumptions:

  • People's behaviour is based on their needs.
  • Needs are in a hierarchical order from basic to higher level.
  • A satisfied need no longer motivates.
  • A person moves to the next higher need only when the lower need is satisfied.

questions.q: Explain any four organisational barriers to communication.
questions.answerHtml:
1. Organisational policy – if the policy does not support free flow of communication, it obstructs effective communication.
  2. Rules and regulations – rigid rules and cumbersome procedures delay communication.
  3. Status – status consciousness creates psychological distance between superiors and subordinates.
  4. Complexity in organisation structure – the more the levels of management, the more the delay and distortion of messages.

questions.q: Meera is the supervisor in a garment unit. She meets workers daily, trains new workers on the stitching machines and settles small disputes. To raise output, the company introduced a bonus for workers exceeding targets, and also started naming the 'Best Tailor of the Month'. (a) Identify the function of management. (b) Identify and explain the elements of this function in the case. (c) Classify the incentives as financial or non-financial.
questions.answerHtml:
(a) Function: Directing.

(b) Elements:

  1. Supervision – 'meets workers daily, trains new workers … settles small disputes'. Supervision means overseeing subordinates at work; the supervisor maintains contact with workers, provides on-the-job training and maintains group unity.
  2. Motivation – 'bonus for workers exceeding targets … Best Tailor of the Month'. Motivation means stimulating people to act to achieve desired goals through incentives.

(c) Incentives:

  • Bonus for exceeding targets – financial incentive (productivity-linked).
  • 'Best Tailor of the Month' – non-financial incentive (employee recognition programme).
